output: This review looked at 22 studies with 763 participants to see if lithium helps people with schizophrenia. Most of the studies were small and not very good. Some studies showed that lithium might help people stay in their studies longer, but this didn't always happen. Other studies found that adding lithium to medicines that already work for schizophrenia might help more people feel better. However, when the studies were looked at more closely, the benefits weren't always clear. The studies also didn't tell us much about the side effects of lithium. Overall, there isn't strong evidence that lithium alone works well for schizophrenia. But adding lithium to other medicines might help some people. More and better studies are needed to learn more about lithium and schizophrenia.

output: This review looked at four studies with a total of 3323 participants, mostly children and adults in hospitals. The studies compared a special plan for keeping patients calm (sedation) given by nurses with regular care. The studies had different levels of quality, but overall, there wasn't strong evidence that the special plan for sedation changed how long patients stayed on machines to help them breathe, their chances of dying in the ICU or hospital, or how long they stayed in the hospital. The special plan did seem to make it less likely that patients would need to be put back on breathing machines (self-extubation) and less likely to need a tracheostomy (a procedure to help breathing). However, the studies didn't show a clear difference in the number of times patients needed to be put back on breathing machines. Overall, there isn't strong evidence to support or refute the use of this special plan for sedation. More studies are needed to better understand its effects and to improve the way they are done to reduce bias.

output: Two studies looked at using tiny worms called Trichuris suis (T. suis) to help people with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). In one study, 54 people with ulcerative colitis (UC) took the worms for 12 weeks. They didn't get better faster than people who took a sugar pill. But 10 out of 30 people who took the worms got much better, compared to 4 out of 24 who took the pill. Another study with 36 people with Crohn's disease (CD) found that taking the worms didn't make their symptoms worse, but 3 out of 27 people who took the worms had side effects, compared to 4 out of 9 who took the pill. Both studies found that the worms helped reduce inflammation in the gut. The studies had low risk of bias, meaning they were done fairly. But the results are not very strong because there weren't many people in the studies. We don't have enough information to say if the worms work well or if they're safe for people with IBD. More studies are needed to learn more about this.

output: This review looked at 23 studies with 2806 people to see if antidepressants helped with sleep problems. Some studies found that antidepressants like paroxetine and trazodone helped people sleep better, especially after 12 weeks. Other antidepressants like doxepin and trazodone also seemed to help, though not always with sleep efficiency or sleep latency. The studies showed that antidepressants like trazodone might help with sleep time, but not always with sleep latency. Most studies didn't report side effects clearly, so it's hard to know if antidepressants cause more side effects than placebos. The evidence isn't strong enough to say for sure if antidepressants work well for sleep problems, especially for longer periods. More high-quality studies are needed to understand if antidepressants are helpful and safe for sleep issues.

output:
This review looked at six studies involving 438 people with neuropathic pain, which is pain caused by damage to nerves. The studies used a medicine called tramadol, starting at a low dose and increasing it over time. Most people in the studies were around 50 to 67 years old, and the studies lasted about four to six weeks. Some people had other health problems, but most did not.

The studies found that tramadol helped reduce pain in about half of the people who took it. This means that out of every 4 people taking tramadol, 1 person got much better. But the studies were small, and the results might not apply to everyone. The researchers think the benefits might be smaller than what the studies show.

Tramadol also caused more side effects than a sugar pill (placebo), like feeling sick or dizzy. About 1 in 4 people taking tramadol had side effects that made them stop taking the medicine, compared to about 1 in 10 people taking the placebo.

Overall, the evidence is not very strong. The studies were small and had some problems that might have led to better results than actually happened. So, while tramadol might help some people with neuropathic pain, we can't be sure it works well for everyone. More studies are needed to know if tramadol is really helpful.

output: This review looked at three studies that compared a type of bone marrow transplant called allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (MSD-HSCT) with another treatment called immunosuppressive therapy for a condition called severe aplastic anemia. output: This review looked at 12 studies comparing different antifungal treatments for eye infections. Most studies had some problems in how they were done, so we can't be sure about their results. But one study found that a treatment called natamycin worked as well as another called voriconazole for healing eye infections. Another study showed that people who got natamycin were more likely to clear the infection completely. Natamycin also seemed to help people see better after the infection. It also helped prevent serious eye problems. However, the studies weren't big enough to tell us if one treatment was clearly better than the others. We don't know if the treatment works differently for different types of fungi. More studies are needed to find out which treatments work best for different types of eye infections.

output: This review looked at 10 studies with 2361 participants that tested whether wearing special stockings called compression stockings can help prevent a condition called PTS after blood clots in the legs (DVT). The studies were not perfect, so we had to use only five of them to get a clearer picture. Wearing these stockings seemed to lower the chance of PTS compared to not wearing them, but it didn't seem to lower the chance of very severe PTS. There wasn't enough information to know if they helped prevent blood clots coming back. Some studies found no difference in PTS between wearing the stockings for a short time or not at all. Other studies suggested that longer wear might help. The stockings didn't seem to affect the chance of getting a blood clot in the lungs. The studies also found that wearing the stockings made people feel better and had better quality of life, but the information wasn't always clear. Some people got itchy or had red skin, but there weren't any serious problems. Most people wore the stockings, but how often varied. While the stockings might help prevent PTS, we need more good studies to be sure.

output: This review looked at three studies comparing milrinone to another medicine called levosimendan, and one study comparing milrinone to a placebo (a pretend medicine). Another study compared milrinone to dobutamine. Milrinone seemed to lower the risk of a condition called low cardiac output syndrome (LCOS) compared to a placebo in one study, but the results weren't clear in other studies. Milrinone didn't seem to affect death rates or other important health outcomes like how long someone stays in the hospital or intensive care. The studies had some problems, so we can't be sure if milrinone helps or not. Some studies showed milrinone might help prevent certain bad side effects, but others didn't find a difference. Overall, there isn't strong evidence to show that milrinone is better than other medicines for preventing LCOS or death in children having heart surgery. More and larger studies are needed to get a clearer picture.

output: This review looked at different types of sealants and fluoride varnishes used to prevent tooth decay in children. Four new studies were added since the last review in 2010. Four studies compared resin-based sealants with fluoride varnishes. They found that resin-based sealants helped prevent tooth decay better than fluoride varnishes in the first permanent molars at two years after application. This finding was supported by one study that lasted longer, showing similar results. Another comparison of two types of glass ionomer sealants didn't show a clear difference in preventing tooth decay. A study that used both sealants and fluoride varnish found that sealants alone worked better than fluoride varnish alone. Overall, the evidence is considered low or very low quality because the studies varied in design and some didn't report all important information. It's hard to say if one type of sealant is definitively better than another. More research is needed to make clearer recommendations.

output: Eight studies with moderate risk of bias looked at how well botulinum toxin A (BtA) injections help people with a condition called cervical dystonia. Most of the studies only included people who had already tried another treatment and worked better for them. The studies gave different amounts of BtA, but mostly used 150 to 236 units of onabotulinumtoxinA (Botox), 120 to 240 units of incobotulinumtoxinA (Xeomin), or 250 to 1000 units of abobotulinumtoxinA (Dysport). After getting the BtA treatment, people reported feeling much better, with an average improvement of about 18.7%. They also said their neck problems were less painful. However, more people experienced side effects like difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) and feeling weak or tired. The studies didn't find a clear link between how much BtA was given and how well it worked. There wasn't enough information to know if one type of BtA was better than another. The studies also didn't look at how BtA affected quality of life or how long the benefits lasted. Because of these limitations, we're moderately sure that BtA helps reduce the symptoms of cervical dystonia, but we're not completely confident that it works better than other treatments. We also know that BtA can cause some side effects, especially difficulty swallowing. More research is needed to figure out the best way to use BtA and how often it should be given.

This review looked at eight studies where people with chronic hepatitis B got acupuncture treatments along with regular care, compared to getting no care at all. Most of these studies had problems that made it hard to trust their results. The studies didn't look at serious bad things that might happen, or how well people felt overall. They also didn't check if the hepatitis B virus went away completely. The studies were small and mostly from one country. 

Acupuncture seemed to help reduce some numbers that show the virus isn't active in the body (HBV DNA), but the evidence for this is very uncertain because the studies were small and not very good. Acupuncture didn't seem to cause more bad side effects than usual care. 

Overall, we don't have enough good evidence to know if acupuncture helps or hurts people with hepatitis B. More studies are needed that are larger, better done, and funded openly. These studies should focus on important outcomes like how people feel and if the virus goes away completely.

output: This review looked at two studies involving 101 patients with ulcerative colitis. One study compared a medicine called methotrexate to a sugar pill (placebo), giving 67 patients methotrexate and 34 patients the placebo. The study that gave methotrexate was done well and didn't have many biases. It found that about half of the patients who took methotrexate and half of those who took the placebo got better and stopped taking steroids. Another study compared methotrexate to another medicine and a dietary supplement. This study wasn't done as well because it wasn't blinded. It found that about half of the patients who took methotrexate and about half of those who took the other medicines got better and stopped taking steroids. The studies didn't find that methotrexate worked better than the other medicines. Some patients had side effects like nausea, rash, and changes in their blood. The studies didn't show that methotrexate helped more than the other medicines. We don't have enough information to know if giving more methotrexate or giving it through a shot might work better. Right now, there's no strong evidence that methotrexate helps start getting better for people with active ulcerative colitis. Larger studies are needed to see if methotrexate works better than other medicines.

This review looked at six studies involving 252 children aged 2.5 to 18 years. The studies mostly compared different ways to stop children from sucking their fingers. Most of the studies had problems doing things correctly, so we can't be sure how good the results really are. The studies followed children for about a year. 

Two studies found that using special mouth devices (like a crib) or a mix of devices and talking to children helped stop finger sucking better than not using anything. Another study found that talking to children and rewarding them for not sucking worked better than not talking to them. 

One study found that using a special mouth device called a palatal crib was better at stopping sucking than another device called a palatal arch. 

Overall, the evidence suggests that special mouth devices and talking to children can help stop finger sucking. But the studies were small and didn't last long enough to know if these methods work well in the long run. We need more high-quality studies to learn more about what works best.

This review looked at 53 studies that involved 105,368 teenagers. Most studies gave both educational talks and helped teens get birth control. When these two things were given together, they seemed to lower the chance of teenagers having an unplanned pregnancy. This happened in four studies, but the difference wasn't big enough to be sure it was real. The studies didn't show much about other things like when teenagers start having sex or how often they use birth control. Some studies had problems, like not checking if the information was true or using different ways to look at the results. 

When just educational talks were given, they didn't seem to make teenagers wait longer to have sex. But they did help teenagers use condoms more often. However, none of the studies checked if these talks reduced unplanned pregnancies. 

Studies that gave birth control advice alone didn't seem to work better than nothing. But giving birth control pills was linked to more teens using them. 

Overall, combining both types of help seems to lower the chance of teenagers having an unplanned pregnancy. But we don't know which type of help works best because the studies were different and not always done the same way. More research is needed to find out which approach is most effective.

This review looked at 17 studies from different countries that involved 919 children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The studies used various methods to help parents interact better with their children, which might improve communication. Some of these studies combined their results to see if they worked better together. The studies had some problems, like not always following the same rules or measuring things the same way.

Overall, the studies didn't show clear benefits for most areas like language and communication skills. But they did find that parent-child interactions became better, especially when parents pay more attention to their children. Parents also reported that their children understood more words. And some children seemed to have fewer autism-related problems.

While these changes are promising, the evidence isn't very strong because the effects were small and the results varied a lot between studies. More research is needed to confirm these findings. 

Parents who use these methods might see less stress, but it's not clear if this happens for everyone. To get better results, researchers should use the same ways to measure outcomes and work together to make sure they're using the best methods.

This review looked at 26 studies with 5299 participants to see if different methods could help more people join and stay in a program called cardiac rehabilitation. Most of the studies were done well, but some had flaws. 

For getting more people into the program, studies showed that certain methods work better. For example, when healthcare providers talk to patients soon after they leave the hospital, it helps more people join. When these talks happen face-to-face, it works even better.

To keep people in the program, studies found that sending reminders or helping them do exercises at home works well. But when the program is spread out across different places, it might not work as well.

The studies didn't find much about problems these methods might cause. Some studies looked at whether these methods helped women or older people more, but they couldn't answer this question clearly because there weren't enough studies.

Overall, we know that these methods can help more people join and stay in the program, but we're not sure how well they work in real-world settings. We need more research to figure out the best ways to make these programs more successful.

output: This review looked at 50 studies with 1916 participants to find out if treatments help reduce itching (pruritus) in different groups of people. Most of the studies had some problems that made it hard to trust their results. The main finding was that paroxetine, a medicine used to treat depression, helped reduce itching in people with advanced illnesses who have different types of itching. Gabapentin, a medicine used to ease nerve pain, also helped reduce itching in people with kidney-related itching. Another medicine called nalfurafine helped reduce itching in people with kidney-related itching too. Cromolyn sodium, a nasal spray, helped reduce itching in people with liver-related itching. Rifampin and flumecinol, medicines used to treat infections, also helped reduce itching in people with liver-related itching. Naltrexone, a medicine used to block opioids, helped reduce itching in people with liver-related itching. But it didn't work as well in people with kidney-related itching. Some other medicines like hydroxyzine, pentoxifylline, triamcinolone, and indomethacin might help reduce itching in people with HIV, but we're not sure because the studies weren't very big or well-designed. Different treatments seemed to work better for different types of itching. More research is needed to find good treatments for itching caused by cancers. Because the studies had some problems, we shouldn't assume these results apply to everyone.

output: This review looked at 21 studies involving 6384 people to see if medicines like methylphenidate and modafinil help with apathy, which is feeling less interested in things and having trouble doing daily tasks, especially in people with Alzheimer's disease (AD). Methylphenidate seemed to help with apathy, making people feel less apathetic, as measured by a tool called the AES. However, it didn't seem to help with another tool called the NPI-apathy subscale. Methylphenidate also seemed to help with thinking and doing daily tasks, but the evidence wasn't very strong. It might also cause some side effects, but not much is known about this. Modafinil didn't show clear benefits for apathy. Other medicines like ChEIs, antipsychotics, and antidepressants weren't studied enough to know if they work. Methylphenidate might help with apathy, but the evidence isn't very strong. More studies are needed to better understand if methylphenidate is helpful for apathy in people with AD.

output: This review looked at 33 studies from different parts of the world, mostly in Asia, that tested how well educating families about pregnancy and childbirth helped new babies. The studies showed that teaching families about these topics reduced the number of newborn deaths, especially in the first few days after birth. It also made more moms get prenatal care and start breastfeeding their babies. However, it didn't seem to help moms use special birth tools or go to doctors when they needed to. The studies found that teaching families these things was usually a good idea because it saves money too. Overall, teaching families about pregnancy and childbirth seems to be helpful in places where it's hard to get doctors and nurses.

output: This review looked at six studies with a total of 3436 participants. Most studies compared different types of medicine to prevent blood clots in people who have had blood clots before. The studies found that none of the medicines tested were better at preventing blood clots or reducing the risk of death compared to a placebo (a sugar pill). Some studies showed that one type of medicine called rivaroxaban might help prevent blood clots, but it didn't seem to cause more bleeding. The studies had some problems, so the results are not very strong. More research is needed to know if these medicines work well and safely for preventing blood clots in people who haven't had blood clots before.

This review looked at nine studies involving 692 people to see if antidepressants helped reduce agitation in people with dementia. The studies found that antidepressants like SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) reduced agitation compared to a sugar pill, as shown by a test called the Cohen-Mansfield Agitation Inventory (CMAI). However, the results were mostly based on one large study. Some studies didn't show a clear benefit for other types of symptoms or for reducing the chance of people leaving the study because of side effects. 

One study found that citalopram, a type of SSRI, might help reduce agitation less than another medicine called risperidone. But it also seemed to cause fewer side effects. Other studies comparing SSRIs to other medicines didn't show much difference in reducing agitation.

Overall, the evidence suggests that SSRIs like sertraline and citalopram may help reduce agitation in people with dementia. But more studies are needed to confirm this and to see if other antidepressants work as well. It's important to note that these studies don't show if these medicines are safe or effective for everyone with dementia.

output: This review looked at five studies that involved 1577 women, mostly those carrying twins or triplets. The studies compared cerclage (a procedure to help keep the cervix closed during pregnancy) with no cerclage. When looking at all the studies together, there wasn't enough evidence to show that cerclage helps prevent deaths or serious problems for babies. For some specific problems like preterm birth or low birth weight, the studies didn't find a clear difference between cerclage and no cerclage. However, the studies found that cerclage might lead to more babies being born too early and having breathing problems. The results are based on a few small studies, so it's hard to be sure if cerclage really helps. There isn't enough information about how well babies do after birth. More research is needed to understand if cerclage is helpful for preventing these problems.

output: This review looked at five studies comparing different treatments for people with severe illness in the hospital. Two studies found that giving extra insulin (a hormone that helps control blood sugar) helped reduce a condition called critical illness-related complications (CIP/CIM), which can happen after major surgery or illness. This extra insulin also helped people stay in the hospital for less time and lowered their chances of dying in the first 180 days. However, using extra insulin can sometimes cause low blood sugar, which needs to be watched carefully. Another study found that giving steroids (another type of medicine) did not help reduce CIP/CIM but did lower the number of times people got new infections. Early physical therapy might help reduce CIP/CIM, but the results weren't clear because the study wasn't done properly. Electrical muscle stimulation didn't seem to help reduce CIP/CIM. The studies that found benefits were large and well-done, but the ones that didn't find benefits were smaller and less clear. More research is needed to confirm these findings and to develop better ways to prevent these complications.

output:
This review looked at five studies with a total of 886 people who had different types of thyroid surgery for a condition called Graves' disease. The studies compared total thyroidectomy (removing the entire thyroid gland), bilateral subtotal thyroidectomy (removing most of the thyroid gland on both sides), and the Dunhill procedure (a less invasive way to remove part of the thyroid). Most of the studies had some problems keeping everything fair, like not making sure doctors didn't know who got which treatment.

Total thyroidectomy was better at preventing a condition called recurrent hyperthyroidism, where the thyroid gland starts working too much again after it was removed. It was also better at preventing this in people who had the Dunhill procedure. However, total thyroidectomy was linked to a higher chance of a condition called permanent hypocalcaemia/hypoparathyroidism, where the body doesn't make enough calcium. This wasn't seen when people had bilateral subtotal thyroidectomy.

The studies didn't look at how well people felt or if the surgeries affected their eyes or voice. One person died in a study, but the researchers didn't have more information about why. The review suggests that total thyroidectomy might be better at preventing hyperthyroidism, but it's not clear if it affects other things like quality of life. More studies are needed to find out.

output: This review looked at 13 studies, mostly done in Italy, to see if a medicine called GHB helps people stop drinking after they've had too much alcohol. GHB seemed to help with withdrawal symptoms like feeling sick, but it caused more dizzy spells. When comparing GHB to another medicine called Clomethiazole, GHB helped more with withdrawal symptoms but caused more side effects. Over time, GHB helped people stay sober better than other medicines. GHB also helped reduce cravings for alcohol. However, there isn't enough strong evidence to say GHB is definitely better than other medicines for treating alcohol withdrawal or preventing relapses. The small amount of studies available suggests that GHB might be helpful in the short term, but more research is needed to confirm these findings. It's important to use GHB under close medical supervision because there are concerns about its potential for addiction and misuse.

output:
This review looked at 1069 studies and found 5 research trials that compared two types of surgery for adrenal gland problems: laparoscopic retroperitoneal adrenalectomy (LRPA) and laparoscopic transperitoneal adrenalectomy (LTPA). About 244 people took part in these trials. The trials lasted from 9 months to 70 months. Most people in the trials were women, and they were around 40 years old.

The trials didn't find clear differences between the two types of surgery for things like how long it takes to feel better after surgery (early morbidity) or how often people have bad side effects (adverse events). But one trial found that people who had LRPA might have fewer late side effects (late morbidity) compared to those who had LTPA. 

People who had LRPA started eating and moving around sooner after surgery. But the evidence for these findings isn't very strong because the trials weren't large enough or well-designed. We don't know if these results will hold true in larger studies.

More research is needed to get a clearer picture of whether LRPA is better than LTPA for things like how long it takes to feel better, how often people have bad side effects, and how much it costs.

This review looked at 27 studies involving 4031 couples or women who were trying to get pregnant using in vitro fertilization (IVF). The studies found that transferring blastocysts (early-stage embryos) instead of cleavage-stage embryos (very early-stage embryos) led to more live births. Specifically, about 32% to 42% of women who got blastocysts transferred ended up having a baby, compared to about 36% who got cleavage-stage embryos. This means more babies were born when blastocysts were used. 

There was no clear difference in how many pregnancies happened overall, whether right away or later, between blastocyst and cleavage-stage transfers. Also, there was no difference in miscarriages. However, fewer embryos were frozen for blastocyst transfers, and more embryos were left unused in blastocyst transfers. 

The evidence isn't very strong because many studies didn't report important information, and some studies might not have been done fairly. So, while blastocyst transfers seem better for getting live births, it's still not clear if they help more with overall pregnancy success. More studies are needed to know for sure.

output: This review looked at six new studies along with previous ones, totaling 16 studies with 2084 participants. Most of the studies had problems in how they were done, so the results should be used with caution. Studies that gave selenium through a vein showed that it might help reduce overall death rates (RR 0.82, meaning about 82% as likely to die). But the results for selenium are mainly based on studies that had some problems. Other studies showed no clear benefit for things like reducing infections or making people stay in the hospital or ICU for shorter times. Selenium didn't seem to cause more bad side effects either. Overall, the evidence isn't strong enough to say that giving selenium to sick people helps them live longer or get better faster. More well-designed studies are needed to figure out if selenium might help.

output: This review looked at six studies that compared gemcitabine to other treatments for bladder cancer. In one study, 341 patients got gemcitabine after surgery, and it didn't help stop tumours coming back compared to a saline solution. But it did reduce the chance of the cancer spreading. Another study found that gemcitabine worked better than another medicine called mitomycin C in preventing tumours from coming back. Gemcitabine caused fewer side effects like burning and needing to urinate more often compared to mitomycin C. In high-risk patients, gemcitabine helped stop tumours from coming back faster but didn't work as well as another medicine called BCG. The studies show that gemcitabine might be helpful, especially for patients whose tumours don't respond to BCG. However, the evidence is not strong because each study had different conditions. More research is needed to confirm these findings. Gemcitabine seems to be a good option to prevent tumours from coming back, but it's not clear if it works better than BCG in all cases.

output:
This review looked at six studies with 2275 participants to see if getting vaccinated helps prevent sickness and death in people who have had cancer. Five studies compared getting vaccinated to not getting vaccinated, and one compared a special type of vaccine (adjuvanted) to a regular vaccine. Most of the studies were done between 1993 and 2015 and involved people with different types of cancers after they had treatments like bone marrow transplants.

For people who got vaccinated compared to those who didn't, the studies showed that getting vaccinated might help reduce sickness and death. Some studies found that vaccinated people had fewer cases of the flu and less pneumonia. One study even showed that vaccinated people stayed in the hospital less often.

However, the evidence isn't very strong because there weren't many studies, and the ones that did exist had some problems. The studies couldn't be sure if the vaccines caused any serious side effects.

For the special type of vaccine, the studies didn't find any big differences in health outcomes. But the evidence here is very uncertain because there were so few studies.

Overall, the studies suggest that getting vaccinated might help prevent sickness and death in people with cancer, but more research is needed to be sure. The evidence is not strong enough to make a clear recommendation about using the special type of vaccine.

output: This review looked at studies about school programs that encourage kids to be more active. It found that these programs helped kids do more physical activities and watch less TV, and their bodies worked better. However, the programs didn't always help kids lose weight or have lower blood pressure. The programs mostly worked well when they were done for at least 12 weeks. But some of the studies might not have been fair because they weren't perfect. The programs still seem helpful, but the effects aren't huge. More research is needed to see how long these benefits last and if they work for everyone.

output: Nine studies looked at combining glaucoma surgery with cataract surgery for people with both conditions. About 650 people took part in the studies, which lasted from 12 to 30 months. The studies were done in different countries, including Europe, Canada, South Africa, and the United States. Most studies found that combining glaucoma surgery with cataract surgery helped lower eye pressure more than just having cataract surgery. This happened in 489 out of 657 eyes studied after one year. Fewer people in the combined surgery group needed to take eye drops to lower their eye pressure after one year. However, the studies didn't tell us if this made a big difference in how well people could see or if it caused more problems during the surgery. The studies weren't sure if combining the surgeries led to needing more operations later or if it caused more problems. The studies also didn't look at how well people felt about their vision or how much it cost. Some people had problems after the surgery, but it wasn't clear if these were more common in the combined surgery group. Overall, the evidence suggests that combining glaucoma surgery with cataract surgery might help lower eye pressure better in the short term, but we're not sure about the long-term effects or if it makes a big difference in how people feel about their vision. More studies are needed to give us a clearer picture.

This review looked at four studies with 253 people who had a condition called pilonidal sinus disease. The studies compared different ways to treat it, using things like a special glue called fibrin glue. Here’s what they found:

- Using fibrin glue instead of another treatment called Bascom's procedure might help reduce pain right after the procedure (a bit), but the evidence isn't very strong.
- Fibrin glue might help people get back to normal activities faster than Bascom's procedure (about 3 weeks faster).
- When used with a type of surgery called the Limberg flap, fibrin glue might make the wound heal faster (by about 14 days).
- It's not clear if fibrin glue helps prevent a common problem called postoperative seroma, which is when fluid builds up in the wound.
- Fibrin glue might also help with pain and getting back to normal activities faster when used with the Limberg flap.
- Adding fibrin glue to the Limberg flap might help people leave the hospital sooner.
- There wasn’t enough information to know if fibrin glue works better than other treatments for preventing a complication called seroma or for reducing the length of time someone stays in the hospital.
- The studies were small and had some problems, so the results aren’t very strong. More and better studies are needed to understand if fibrin glue really helps with these conditions.

output:
This study looked at three trials that tested different antibiotic treatments for women having normal births. The trials happened in different places and times, mostly in the 1960s and 1990s. The main finding was that women who got antibiotics had a lower chance of getting a type of infection called endometritis, which is an infection of the lining of the uterus. This was true in two out of the three trials, but the evidence isn't very strong because there weren't many women in the study and the results were a bit uncertain. 

There wasn't much difference between the groups for other types of infections like urinary tract infections or wound infections. The women who got antibiotics stayed in the hospital for about the same amount of time. Antibiotics cost more money, about twice as much.

The trials didn't look at whether antibiotics caused side effects or if they helped women feel better. They also didn't check if using antibiotics made it harder for germs to become resistant to medicines. 

While antibiotics might help prevent one type of infection, they don't seem to help with other types of infections or make women stay in the hospital longer. It's important to use antibiotics carefully because overusing them can lead to germs becoming resistant to medicine. More studies are needed to see if giving antibiotics to all women after normal births is helpful.

output: This review looked at 177 studies with 34,808 participants to see if certain treatments helped with psoriasis. For most vitamin D medicines applied to the body, they worked better than a sugar pill. This means people felt better, with scores improving by about 0.8 to 1.9 points on a scale. Potent and very potent corticosteroids also worked well, helping people feel better by about 1.0 to 1.8 points. Other treatments like dithranol, combined vitamin D and corticosteroid, and tazarotene were also better than a sugar pill. When comparing vitamin D to strong corticosteroids, the results were mixed. But when using both vitamin D and corticosteroid together, it worked better than just vitamin D or just corticosteroid. Vitamin D was less effective for scalp psoriasis compared to strong corticosteroids. Strong corticosteroids caused fewer skin problems like burning or irritation. They were also easier to use than vitamin D alone. However, there's not enough information to know if using strong corticosteroids long-term might cause changes to the skin. More research is needed to understand this better and to find safe ways to treat psoriasis over time.

output: Nine studies looked at whether putting patients in the prone position (on their stomachs) while they are on a breathing machine helps them live longer. Most of the studies were similar because they all involved patients with breathing problems who needed machines to help them breathe. The studies found that putting patients in the prone position might make it a little bit easier for them to breathe, but it didn't seem to save more lives overall. Some studies showed that putting patients in the prone position for longer periods of time or for patients who were very sick when they started might help them live longer. However, the evidence isn't strong enough to say for sure if this works. There were also some side effects like pressure sores and problems with the breathing tube. More studies are needed to know if putting patients in the prone position really helps or if it causes more problems.

output: Three studies involving 105 participants looked at whether methadone helps people with nerve pain. These studies were done differently and had some problems, so we can't be sure about their results. The studies mainly compared methadone to a sugar pill. Some people who got methadone said their pain was less, but it wasn't clear if this happened to enough people to show a real difference. The studies didn't tell us if methadone caused more bad side effects than the sugar pill. Because of these issues, we don't think the studies give us good information about whether methadone works better than other treatments for nerve pain. There just isn't enough reliable data to make a decision about methadone for nerve pain.

output: This review looked at 106 studies that tested different ways to check for glaucoma in the eyes. It involved 16,260 eyes in total. The studies used three main methods: GDx, HRT, and OCT. GDx had the best results, especially for a part called the Nerve Fibre Indicator. HRT and OCT also worked well, but not as much as GDx. When checking for glaucoma, these tests can sometimes miss some cases where glaucoma is present (false negatives) or wrongly show glaucoma in people who don't have it (false positives). This happens more often in people with more advanced glaucoma. The studies had some problems, like using a type of study design that might make the results look better than they really are. To get clearer information, more studies are needed that use real-world patients and describe why they were checked for glaucoma.

output:
This review looked at nine studies involving 1354 participants who were given vitamin B or its derivatives along with a placebo or another treatment. Most studies lasted from two to 36 months. Some studies didn't clearly show if they were fair in their comparisons. About half of the studies said they tried to keep people from knowing who got which treatment, but not all did. Some studies had problems keeping people in the study, and others might have had problems reporting their results. Funding for some studies came from companies that make vitamin B products, which could have affected how they were done.

The studies found that vitamin B or its combinations didn't help reduce kidney damage (called diabetic kidney disease or DKD) or improve kidney function. They didn't find that vitamin B helped lower blood pressure or reduce the risk of dying from any cause. Some studies saw that taking thiamine (a type of vitamin B) might help lower a marker of kidney damage called albumin in the urine. But taking vitamin B or its combinations didn't seem to help with kidney function or blood pressure.

Taking thiamine alone seemed to help lower albumin in the urine, but it didn't affect kidney function or blood pressure. Overall, there's not enough good evidence to recommend using vitamin B or its combinations to treat DKD. More studies are needed to confirm these findings because the studies were small and had some flaws.

output: This review looked at 100 studies involving more than 83,000 mother-infant pairs. Most of the studies had some issues in how they were done, but the overall picture is clear: extra support for mothers helps keep them breastfeeding longer and more exclusively. This support can come from doctors, nurses, or other helpers. Studies show that extra support reduces the chances of moms stopping breastfeeding altogether, and also keeps moms from stopping exclusive breastfeeding (when only breast milk is given). The benefits are seen whether the support comes from professionals or non-professionals, or both. To work best, the support should be offered regularly, like once every few weeks, and tailored to the mom's needs and the place where she lives. It's also helpful if the support is given by someone who has talked to the mom before, like her doctor or nurse. Overall, extra support seems to help moms keep breastfeeding longer and more exclusively.

output: This review looked at two studies that found ifosfamide helped people live longer with advanced lung cancer. It also found that chemotherapy drugs like methotrexate, doxorubicin, and topotecan might help people live longer after their cancer comes back. However, these studies had some problems, so we're not sure how much better these treatments really are. The chemotherapy caused more side effects, but it didn't seem to make people feel worse overall. Some studies from the 1970s suggested ifosfamide might help people live longer, but newer studies show that combining platinum-based drugs with other chemotherapy drugs can help people respond better to treatment without making them sicker. Overall, the evidence isn't strong, and more studies are needed to understand the best way to treat advanced lung cancer.

output: This review looked at 32 studies comparing a medication called pimozide to other treatments for people with schizophrenia. Most studies didn't have enough information to show if pimozide helped reduce symptoms like feeling better or having fewer bad thoughts. Some studies found that pimozide might help with movement problems, but the results weren't always clear. There wasn't enough good-quality evidence to say if pimozide improves quality of life or helps prevent relapses of symptoms. When pimozide was used along with other antipsychotic medications, it seemed to help prevent relapses of symptoms better than just using other antipsychotic medications. Overall, the evidence suggests that pimozide works similarly to other common antipsychotic medications, but more research is needed to know if it's better for everyone with schizophrenia. It doesn't seem to be helpful for people with delusional disorder.

output: This review looked at 26 studies with 17,578 people to see if a quick way to tell partners about infections (expedited partner notification or EPN) works better than just telling the person who has the infection (simple patient referral). For infections like urethritis or cervicitis, EPN was better at stopping the infection coming back to the person who first got it. It also made more partners get treatment. But for chlamydia, it didn't work better. EPN didn't work better than just telling the person who has the infection in some cases. EPN helped more partners get treated for some infections, but not others. Sometimes, EPN didn't make more partners get tested or treated. We don't know which parts of EPN work best. More studies are needed to find out which methods work best for different infections.

The studies compared CT to different things like regular care, other types of therapy, or no treatment at all. Some studies didn't do a good job hiding who got which treatment, which might have affected the results. 

For CT to help with overall thinking skills, the studies showed it works a little bit better than usual care. It also helped with remembering words. But, we're not sure if CT helps with other thinking skills or makes people feel better.

But, we're not very confident about these findings because the studies weren't perfect. Future studies should try harder to make sure the results are fair and look at how CT compares to other treatments.

output: This review looked at 27 studies involving 8244 people who had surgery. The studies compared different types of medicine called nitrates (like nitroglycerin, isosorbide dinitrate, and nicorandil) with no treatment, placebo, or other medicines. Most of the surgeries were done on older adults. Some studies used special medicine to help people sleep during surgery. The studies mostly looked at how well people did after surgery, like if they had heart problems or died. The results showed that taking nitrates didn't seem to make it less likely that people would die or have heart problems right after their surgery. However, one study suggested that nicorandil might help prevent heart problems, but the evidence wasn't strong enough to be sure. The studies had some problems, so the results aren't very strong. More research is needed to know if nitrates help or hurt people having surgery that isn't on their heart.

output: This review looked at 83 studies with 10,036 people to see if certain treatments helped clear skin problems. Most studies didn't fully describe how they did things, which made it hard to compare them. Four types of treatments—3% diclofenac in 2.5% hyaluronic acid, 0.5% 5-fluorouracil, 5% imiquimod, and 0.025% to 0.05% ingenol mebutate—were found to work better than placebos or other treatments for clearing skin problems. Photodynamic therapy (PDT) using aminolevulinic acid (ALA) or methyl aminolevulinate (MAL) was also found to be better than placebo-PDT. Cryotherapy was less effective. The studies showed that these treatments worked better in clearing skin problems, but some people had side effects like feeling sick or having redness. Some treatments like imiquimod and PDT had better-looking results after treatment. More studies are needed to decide which treatment might work best for each person.

output: This review looked at 47 studies with 17,039 participants to see if a medicine called clonidine, used to help calm nerves, helps reduce problems after surgeries. For surgeries that aren't on the heart, clonidine didn't seem to help lower the chance of dying or having a heart attack. It did make it less likely that someone would have a big drop in their heartbeat, which can be dangerous. Clonidine also made it more likely that someone would have a drop in blood pressure, which can be uncomfortable. For heart surgeries, there wasn't enough information to know if clonidine helped or hurt. Overall, clonidine doesn't seem to be helpful for preventing major problems after surgeries, but it can cause some side effects like drops in heartbeat and blood pressure. More research is needed to better understand its effects.

Three trials involving 1694 people looked at whether alemtuzumab or interferon beta-1a helps treat multiple sclerosis (MS). Alemtuzumab is given as daily injections or yearly IV treatments, while interferon beta-1a is given as weekly injections. The trials had some problems in how they were done, which might affect the results. 

Alemtuzumab at a lower dose (12 mg/day) seemed to help reduce the number of MS attacks and the worsening of disability compared to interferon beta-1a. It also seemed to help reduce new areas of damage seen on MRI scans. But it wasn't clear if it helped with disability scores after 3 years. 

Alemtuzumab at a higher dose (24 mg/day) also seemed to help reduce MS attacks and disability worsening. Serious side effects were common in both groups, but the chance of having them was about the same. 

Overall, alemtuzumab seems to help with MS symptoms and reduce attacks and new brain damage, but more research is needed to confirm these findings. People using alemtuzumab need close monitoring for possible serious side effects.

output: This review looked at six trials with 885 patients to see if adding a vein cuff to a prosthetic graft helps improve blood flow after surgery for leg problems. Some trials showed that adding a vein cuff might help keep the graft open longer, especially for below-the-knee bypasses. However, other trials didn't find a clear benefit. The evidence isn't strong enough to say for sure that adding a vein cuff makes a big difference. More research is needed to confirm these findings, especially focusing on below-the-knee grafts.

This review looked at 10 studies involving 840 people to see if continuing or maintaining treatments helped prevent heart problems after depression. Most studies were done fairly well, but some had issues like not keeping who got what treatment secret. 

For continuing treatments, people taking medicine to help with depression were less likely to have their depression come back or get worse compared to those taking a sugar pill. But the studies weren't perfect, so we're not sure if this really works. 

For maintaining treatments, the studies didn't show much difference between medicine and a placebo. Some studies suggested that continuing therapy might help, but the evidence wasn't strong enough to be sure. 

Overall, we don't have good proof that continuing or maintaining medicines or therapy helps prevent depression coming back or getting worse. We need more studies to learn more about this.

This review looked at seven studies with 345 patients to see if early feeding (early enteral nutrition) helps or hurts people who are sick and need to be in the hospital. The studies were not all done the same way, so we can't be sure about their results. 

For early feeding compared to waiting to feed, we're not sure if it makes a big difference in how soon people die (mortality). Some studies said it might help, but others didn't find a difference. There's also uncertainty about whether it causes more infections or problems with eating and digestion. 

Early feeding compared to delayed feeding with extra nutrients (parenteral nutrition) also wasn't clearly better or worse for death, infections, or how long people stayed in the hospital. 

Overall, the evidence is very shaky, like looking through a foggy window. We need bigger, better studies to get clearer answers about whether early feeding helps or harms people in the hospital.

output: This review looked at seven studies involving 1839 people with heart problems who were randomly assigned to different treatments. Most of the studies had some problems, like not treating everyone equally. The studies found that people who got treatment at home using a medicine called LMWH were less likely to have blood clots come back compared to those who got the same medicine in a hospital. There wasn't much difference in things like bleeding or death. Some people said they felt better at home. But the studies weren't perfect, so we don't know if home treatment is definitely better. It seems that home treatment might be the way of the future because more people are getting it. Now, doctors are working on making sure home treatment works well and is safe for everyone.

We also don't know if screening everyone for skin cancer works. More research is needed to find out if screening for skin cancer is helpful or harmful.

output: A study found that a medicine called pembrolizumab might help people with advanced bladder cancer live longer. It probably reduces the chance of dying from any cause (115 fewer deaths out of every 1000 people with bladder cancer who get the medicine at 12 months). Pembrolizumab might also make it easier for people to feel better and do daily activities. It may not stop the cancer from getting worse, but it might make the cancer go away a bit better. Using pembrolizumab might make it less likely that the cancer will come back and cause problems. It might also make it less likely that the person will stop taking the medicine because of side effects. However, we're not sure if it makes a big difference in how often serious side effects happen. Overall, the study suggests that pembrolizumab might be a good choice for some people with advanced bladder cancer who have already tried another type of medicine. But we don't know for sure because it's just one study, and the company that makes the medicine paid for it.

output: This review looked at three studies that tested a drug called aripiprazole in children and teenagers with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The studies found that aripiprazole helped reduce certain behaviors like irritability, hyperactivity, and repetitive actions. It also caused some side effects like weight gain and sleepiness. The studies were mostly done well, but one had missing information. The benefits of aripiprazole seem to last for about 8 weeks. However, after that time, some children might have their old symptoms come back. Also, the way doctors diagnose ASD has changed since these studies were done. So, more research is needed to see if aripiprazole works long-term and if it's safe for everyone with ASD.

This review looked at 42 studies with 3262 participants. Most studies had some problems in how they were done, which makes it hard to trust the results fully. 

For people using a special fluid called neutral pH, low GDP during their daily kidney dialysis (PD), the studies showed that this fluid helped keep their kidneys working better (residual renal function) and kept more urine in their bodies. This happened more over time. But the studies weren't perfect, so we're not sure how much better it really makes things.

For those using a different fluid called icodextrin, the studies suggested it might help keep people from getting too full with fluid during their dialysis, and it might help remove more fluid from their bodies. But we're not sure if it helps with other things like infections or making people feel bad.

Overall, the studies show that using neutral pH, low GDP fluid seems to help keep the kidneys working well and keeps more urine out. Using icodextrin fluid might help with fluid management, but we need more good studies to know for sure if it helps with other things.

output: This review looked at 35 studies involving 5108 participants to see if using two-dimensional ultrasound helps during a procedure called central venous catheterization, which is used to give fluids or medicine through a vein. The studies found that using two-dimensional ultrasound helped reduce complications overall by about 71%, and it also reduced the number of times an artery was accidentally punctured. It made it easier to successfully insert the catheter, reducing the number of attempts needed by about 20%. It also made it more likely that the catheter would be inserted successfully on the first try by about 57%. Using ultrasound also seemed to lower the risk of bleeding around the area where the catheter was inserted. The ultrasound helped speed up the process too, making it about 30 seconds faster on average. While ultrasound didn't seem to affect the overall success rate or the number of complications, it did help in some specific areas like reducing the risk of bleeding and making the first attempt more successful. However, the evidence wasn't strong enough to compare how well ultrasound works for experienced or inexperienced doctors or for people who might have a higher risk of complications. More research is needed to fully understand the benefits of using ultrasound in these situations.

output: Seven studies with 538 participants who had chronic hepatitis C were reviewed. Most of the studies had a high risk of having some mistakes in their methods. The studies compared a medicine called nitazoxanide with a sugar pill or no treatment at all. Nitazoxanide seemed to help people with hepatitis C feel better and their livers worked a little better, but it didn't seem to make them live longer. It didn't seem to cause more side effects than the sugar pill. Studies showed that people who took nitazoxanide were less likely to have their virus come back after treatment. However, the evidence for this isn't very strong because the studies had some problems. Nitazoxanide didn't seem to help with a common blood test that measures liver health. The studies couldn't tell if nitazoxanide helped with other important things like how well people felt or if it made their liver disease worse. We don't know if nitazoxanide works for people with different types of hepatitis C. More studies are needed to find out if nitazoxanide helps people with chronic hepatitis C.

This review looked at three studies involving 350 women who had gone through menopause. The studies compared hormone replacement therapy (HRT) with women who didn't get HRT. The women were followed for different lengths of time, from about 3 years to almost 20 years. The studies were done in different places around the world, including Europe, South Africa, and China. 

The studies found that HRT might help women live longer (overall survival), but it's not clear if it makes their lives better (quality of life). It might also help prevent some health problems like blood clots and heart attacks, but the evidence isn't strong enough to say for sure. 

There wasn't enough information to know if HRT increases the chance of getting breast cancer or causes gallstones. Some studies suggested it might slightly lower the chance of having a stroke or heart attack, but the evidence wasn't very strong. 

Overall, the evidence is not very strong because there weren't many studies or people involved. More research is needed to understand if HRT helps or harms women after they've had surgery for ovarian cancer.

output: This review looked at three trials involving 20,412 women who had heavy bleeding after childbirth (postpartum haemorrhage or PPH). Two of the trials compared a medicine called tranexamic acid (TXA) given through a vein (intravenous) with a placebo or usual care. The largest trial, called the WOMAN trial, found that women who got TXA had a lower risk of dying from bleeding compared to those who didn't get it. This was true whether the TXA was given right away or later. Women who got TXA also lost less blood overall. However, TXA didn't seem to help prevent serious health problems like needing a blood transfusion or having surgery to stop the bleeding. It did make it more common to use special stitches to close the uterus. The evidence is mostly good, but some parts are a bit uncertain. More research is needed to find out if giving TXA earlier works better.

This review looked at 14 studies involving 2165 women. The studies compared different ways of transferring embryos during in-vitro fertilization (IVF). Three studies compared repeated single embryo transfers (SET) with doing just one cycle of deep cleavage stage embryo transfer (DET). When these studies were combined, there was no clear difference in the number of babies born, but there were fewer twins and triplets born with SET. 

Ten studies compared doing just one cycle of SET with doing just one cycle of DET. Again, there was no clear difference in the number of babies born, but there were fewer twins and triplets born with SET. 

For women who want to have one baby, it seems that having just one cycle of SET instead of one cycle of DET might result in a slightly lower chance of having a baby, but also a lower chance of having twins or triplets. 

Overall, having just one cycle of SET might help reduce the risk of having too many babies, but it might also slightly lower the chance of having a baby. More research is needed to confirm these findings, especially in older women.

This review looked at 29 studies that tested whether taking fish oil supplements could help people who have had a stroke. Most of the studies had good methods, but some were small. The studies lasted from a few weeks to more than a year. 

For short-term use (less than three months), there wasn't enough good evidence to show that fish oil helps with how well someone can do daily tasks or their mood. Some studies suggested it might help a little bit, but the results weren't clear.

For longer-term use (more than three months), there was some evidence that fish oil might help with how well someone can move around and do daily tasks. But again, the evidence isn't strong. 

There were also some side effects reported, like bleeding, but they weren't common. 

Overall, the evidence is not very strong, and more studies are needed to know if fish oil helps after a stroke. These studies should start soon after a stroke happens and use clear ways to measure how well people are doing. More research is also needed to figure out the best dose and how to take the fish oil.

output:
This review looked at six studies with 10,018 people to see if sulfonylureas or meglitinides helped manage type 2 diabetes. The studies lasted from 6 months to 5 years. None of the studies were done well enough to give us very strong confidence in their results. 

For sulfonylureas, like glimepiride, there wasn't much evidence of them causing death or major health problems. But there was a bit of mixed evidence about whether they might help prevent type 2 diabetes. Some studies said yes, others said no. It's hard to tell because the studies didn't always use the same way to check for type 2 diabetes.

Nateglinide, another type of medicine, seemed to have a small chance of helping with type 2 diabetes. About 36 out of 100 people taking it got type 2 diabetes, compared to 33 out of 100 taking a placebo. But the study wasn't big enough to know if this was really helpful.

Nateglinide also seemed to cause a few more serious health problems, like heart attacks and strokes, but not enough to be sure it was harmful. It didn't seem to affect the chances of needing hospital care for heart problems.

Overall, the studies weren't large enough or done well enough to show clearly if sulfonylureas or nateglinide help prevent type 2 diabetes or its problems. More studies are needed to find out.

output: This review looked at 21 studies to see if certain road changes help keep cyclists safer. Most studies didn't find that adding special bike lanes or using different colors for bikes helped prevent crashes. Some studies suggested that having bike-only routes might make it safer for cyclists, but others said it might not. Using 20 mph zones in cities seemed to help reduce crashes. Changing some parts of bike routes that have lots of cars could make them safer. Converting some intersections to roundabouts, which are like circles where cars go around, might actually cause more crashes. Adding bike lanes across street corners or putting bike paths next to roads might make cyclists more likely to get hurt. But these ideas aren't very clear because the studies weren't always done well. There's not enough good evidence to say for sure if these changes really help keep cyclists safe. More studies are needed to figure out the best ways to make roads safer for cyclists.

output: This review looked at 71 studies comparing different antipsychotic medications: chlorpromazine, olanzapine, risperidone, and quetiapine. None of the studies looked at costs. In the short term, olanzapine seemed to work better than chlorpromazine for improving how people feel, but it didn't help prevent their condition from coming back. Chlorpromazine caused more side effects like muscle problems, but people felt better overall with olanzapine. With risperidone, there wasn't much difference between chlorpromazine and risperidone, and both worked similarly well. Risperidone made people feel better overall. Chlorpromazine and quetiapine didn't seem to differ much in how well they worked, but people taking quetiapine had better quality of life scores. Chlorpromazine caused more muscle problems. Most of the studies were done in China with hospital patients, so the results might not apply to everyone else. The studies were mostly short-term, so we don't know if these medications work differently over time. Chlorpromazine seems to cause more side effects, but the studies used different doses, so it's hard to say exactly why.

output:
This review looked at one study that gave calcium supplements to women before and during pregnancy to see if it helps prevent problems like pre-eclampsia, which is a condition where a woman's blood pressure gets too high during pregnancy. The study involved about 1355 women in different countries. 

The study found that taking calcium before and during pregnancy might not help prevent pre-eclampsia, but it might slightly lower the chance of having a baby born too early or losing the baby. It also didn't seem to affect the risk of other problems like needing a cesarean section or having a baby born underweight.

The study also didn't find strong evidence that calcium helps with other things like the baby's birth weight, how early the baby is born, or if the baby needs special care after birth. The study wasn't perfect because some women dropped out before the end of the study.

Overall, the evidence isn't strong enough to say that giving calcium before or during pregnancy definitely helps or hurts. More research is needed to know if starting calcium before or during pregnancy can help prevent problems for mom and baby.

output: This review looked at different ways to help people who smoke cut down or switch to safer cigarettes. Most of the studies tested nicotine replacement therapy (NRT), like gum or inhalers, which helped people reduce the number of cigarettes they smoke. Using NRT increased the chance of cutting down by half or more compared to a placebo (a fake treatment). It also increased the chance of quitting smoking. However, the evidence for other methods like bupropion, varenicline, e-cigarettes, and snus is not clear and may not work better than other treatments. Some studies showed that these methods might help reduce harmful chemicals in the smoke, but it's not clear if this would make a big difference in health. The studies had some problems, like not always being fair to both groups or not knowing who was getting the real treatment. Overall, the evidence suggests that NRT can help people cut down and quit smoking, but we're not sure about other methods. More high-quality studies are needed to know if these other methods work and if they can help people stay healthy.

output: This review looked at five trials involving 297 women with a type of abnormal cells in their vagina called high-grade VIN. Three trials were considered to have a low to moderate risk of having mistakes in their results. The trials compared different treatments for these cells. Topical imiquimod, which is a cream applied to the skin, seemed to work better than a placebo cream. Women who used the imiquimod cream were more likely to get better, both at five to six months and at one year. They also had fewer problems like redness, soreness, and itching. However, the treatment might cause some women to need lower doses. The review found that imiquimod worked as well as another medicine called cidofovir, but more information is needed to know if it works better in the long run. Another medicine called indole-3-carbinol was tested in just one trial, and the results were not clear. Overall, imiquimod seems to be a safe and effective treatment for high-grade VIN, but more research is needed to confirm its long-term benefits and whether it helps prevent cancer.

output: This review looked at 19 studies with 1870 women who had hysteroscopy. Misoprostol was found to be more effective than no treatment or placebo for making the cervix open wider before surgery. Women using misoprostol needed less help to open their cervix during surgery. They also had fewer problems during the procedure, like cuts or getting lost inside the uterus. Misoprostol caused some extra discomfort, like stomach pain and bleeding. It worked better than another medicine called dinoprostone, but it caused more side effects. Another medicine called osmotic dilators, which are like little water balloons, didn't seem to work as well as misoprostol. Overall, misoprostol seems to be a good choice for preparing the cervix before surgery, but it causes more side effects. More studies are needed to confirm these findings.

output: This review looked at four studies comparing different antibiotics for treating chlamydia (CT) infections. For men, taking azithromycin instead of doxycycline did not seem to help much more against the bacteria causing the infection (microbiological failure), but it might cause fewer side effects. For women, the studies weren't clear about whether azithromycin works better or worse. The studies didn't look at whether the antibiotics caused the bacteria to become resistant or if the infections came back. The most common side effects were not serious and related to the stomach. For men, using azithromycin might not be as good as using doxycycline. For women, we're not sure if azithromycin works better or worse. Doxycycline might work better than ofloxacin for both men and women. The studies didn't find out if doxycycline worked better or worse for men or women. To get clearer answers, more studies are needed, especially ones that include more women and look at things like whether the bacteria become resistant or if the infections come back. It would also be helpful to study how well people take the medicine and if it causes side effects.

output: One study found that using a special ultrasound (EAUS) before repairing a second-degree tear in the perineum (the area between the vagina and anus) helped reduce the chance of having severe problems with leaking stool or gas in the first six months after giving birth. This was true for about half as many women as in the group that just used a regular check. However, more women in the group that used the ultrasound said they had pain in the area right after birth. The study involved 752 women, which is not a very big group. The results might not apply to all women, especially those who have given birth before. More research is needed to confirm these findings and see if the ultrasound helps prevent problems in the long run.

output:
This review looked at 14 studies with a total of 978 children who had kidney or ureter stones. The studies were not always done well, so we can't be sure if shock wave lithotripsy (SWL) works better than other treatments. Here's what we know:

- SWL might help remove more stones from the kidneys, but it doesn't seem to cause more problems.
- SWL might help with pain, but it's not clear if it causes more serious problems.
- SWL might lead to more follow-up treatments, like taking medicine to help pass stones.
- Sometimes, SWL doesn't work as well as another procedure called percutaneous nephrolithotripsy (PCNL).
- PCNL might be less effective than a newer type of PCNL that doesn't use tubes.
- Alpha-blockers, which are medicines that relax the bladder neck, might help remove more stones, but we're not sure if they cause more problems.

Overall, we're not very confident in these results because the studies weren't always done well. More high-quality studies are needed to give us clearer answers about what works best for children with kidney and ureter stones.

output: This review looked at 10 studies with 697 children who received psychological therapy for various health problems like headaches, arthritis, sickle cell disease, and stomach pain. The studies mostly had low risks of bias, but some aspects were unclear. For headache problems, the therapy helped reduce pain and made it easier to do daily activities. It didn't help with feelings of sadness or worry. For other types of chronic pain, the therapy didn't seem to help with pain or make daily activities easier. The therapy didn't cause major side effects, and most kids said they liked it. There are still not enough studies to know if the therapy works well for everyone. More research is needed to better understand if this therapy helps children with different health issues.

output: One study found that giving people a special test before starting a medicine called abacavir might help prevent a bad reaction to the medicine. This study involved 1956 adults with HIV who were about to start abacavir. The study divided the participants into two groups. One group got the special test before starting abacavir, and the other group started the medicine without the test. The group that got the test first was less likely to have a severe reaction to the medicine. About 43% fewer people in the test group had a severe reaction compared to those who didn't get the test. The study was funded by the company that makes abacavir. While the study suggests that the test might help, it wasn't perfect. Some people dropped out of the study, and the doctors who diagnosed the reactions might have been influenced by their own experience. The study found that the test probably helps reduce severe skin reactions to abacavir, but more research is needed to confirm this. The study's results are considered moderate-quality, meaning they're somewhat reliable but not perfect. More studies are needed to see if this test works for other medicines and in different groups of people.

output:
This review looked at 55 studies involving 5417 women who had different surgeries for stress urinary incontinence. Most surgeries, like open retropubic colposuspension, helped women feel better and have less leaking. Compared to other surgeries, open retropubic colposuspension worked well in the long run, especially in the first five years. It also seemed to work better than traditional slings in the long term. Women who had needle suspensions had fewer leaks after the first year compared to those who had open colposuspension. 

However, newer surgeries called TVT and laparoscopic colposuspension might be cheaper in the long run, but we don't know if they're as good as open colposuspension. Also, these newer surgeries might cause more problems with emptying your bladder. 

Overall, open retropubic colposuspension seems to be a good option for treating stress urinary incontinence, especially for the long term. But it might lead to more problems with your uterus falling down. Laparoscopic colposuspension might be faster to recover from, but we need more information about how well it works in the long term.

output:
This review looked at seven studies with 1074 children and teenagers who had a type of arthritis that lasted a long time. The studies compared different types of medicine called NSAIDs with other medicines. Most studies didn't have a fair comparison because they didn't use a placebo. The studies had different levels of quality, meaning some were better than others. 

For how much better the medicines made the pain go away, the studies weren't clear if the NSAIDs worked better than other medicines. Some studies showed the NSAIDs helped a bit, but it wasn't enough to be sure. Other studies showed that different doses of one NSAID might work similarly to another NSAID.

The studies also found that some children experienced side effects like feeling dizzy or having upset stomachs. But the studies couldn't tell if these side effects were caused by the medicines or just happened by chance.

There wasn't enough information to say if the NSAIDs helped or hurt the children's ability to move around, sleep, or feel good overall. Also, there wasn't enough information to say if the children liked taking the medicines or if they helped their daily activities or overall health.

Overall, the evidence isn't strong enough to say if NSAIDs help or hurt children with this type of arthritis. More studies are needed to learn more.

output: This review looked at 39 studies with 3520 participants. It found that amifostine, when given during radiation therapy for cancer, might help prevent a dry mouth (xerostomia) for up to three months after treatment. This was true for 2 out of 3 studies that could be combined to look at this effect. Amifostine also seemed to help increase saliva production for up to 12 months after treatment. However, there isn't enough evidence to know if this helps prevent the spread of cancer or improves quality of life. Amifostine can cause some side effects like nausea, vomiting, and changes in blood pressure. Some studies showed that amifostine might improve quality of life for up to 12 months after treatment. Other treatments like pilocarpine and palifermin didn't seem to work better or worse than amifostine. Overall, amifostine seems to help prevent a dry mouth, but more research is needed to see if it has lasting benefits or affects other aspects of health.
