output: This review looked at five new trials, bringing the total to 12 studies with 2300 participants who had oral cavity cancer. Most of the studies had some problems in how they were done, so we can't be very sure of their results. The studies mostly compared different types of neck surgery for people with oral cavity cancer who didn't have cancer in their neck yet. Some studies found that doing the neck surgery right away might help people live longer, but other studies weren't clear. Other studies found that doing the neck surgery right away didn't make a difference. The studies also looked at whether the surgery helped prevent the cancer coming back in the neck area. Overall, the evidence isn't strong enough to tell us which type of neck surgery is best. There wasn't enough good information to know if adding radiation therapy to surgery helps or hurts. The studies also didn't give us much information about how well people felt or how their lives changed after the surgery. More research is needed to better understand the best way to treat neck areas in people with oral cavity cancer.

output: This review looked at two out of three studies that compared two medications, carbamazepine and topiramate, for treating seizures. About 93% of the people who took part in the studies had seizures that started in one part of their brain (focal seizures). The study found that carbamazepine might help people with focal seizures stay seizure-free longer and reach a state where they don't have seizures (remission) sooner than topiramate. However, the study wasn't sure if topiramate was better for preventing the first seizure or if it worked better for stopping seizures caused by side effects. The study also found that both medications can cause side effects like feeling sleepy, headaches, and upset stomach, but these happen about the same amount with both drugs. The study's findings are mostly useful for people with focal seizures. The evidence for people with generalised seizures (where the whole body shakes) or unclassified seizures (whose type isn't clear) is less strong because there weren't enough people in those groups. The researchers think the results might change with more studies. Future studies should be done carefully to get clearer answers.

output:
This review looked at 33 studies that tested different ways to encourage people to be more physically active in their communities. Most of the studies tried to build partnerships with local government or non-profit organizations. About half of the studies took place in high-income countries, and the rest in low-income countries. The studies varied in how much they focused on different activities and how strong those activities were. 

Most of the studies didn't look at whether the programs helped people who were less wealthy or had other challenges. Only a few studies said they worked with these groups. Many of the studies had problems because they weren't done very well, especially in how they picked which communities got the new activities.

The studies that were done better didn't show that the new activities made people more active overall. Some studies did find that more people started walking in the areas where the new activities were happening. But these changes weren't seen in the whole community. 

Overall, the studies didn't show that big community-wide programs make people more active. There were some exceptions, like in China where more people walked, but these were rare. The studies also had trouble showing if the programs were worth the money spent on them. Some studies didn't tell us about any bad effects. The information we do have isn't consistent, which makes it hard to know if these programs work.

output: This review looked at 36 studies involving 2377 participants to see if L-ornithine L-aspartate helps treat or prevent liver problems. Most of the studies found that L-ornithine L-aspartate helped reduce liver swelling (hepatic encephalopathy) and improve heart function. However, the studies weren't all done the same way, so we're not sure how well it works. L-ornithine L-aspartate seemed to help lower the chance of dying, but we're not completely sure because the evidence isn't very strong. It might also help with serious side effects, but we're not certain. The studies didn't find much difference in how it affects other common side effects like feeling sick. When compared to other treatments, L-ornithine L-aspartate didn't seem to work better for reducing the chance of getting sick or having serious side effects. More studies are needed to confirm these findings.

output: This review looked at 11 studies involving 669 people with seizures. The studies compared two medicines, phenytoin and sodium valproate, to see which works better. The results show that people taking phenytoin might stop responding to the medicine sooner for reasons like side effects or the medicine not working well. But it's not clear if this happens more often. Sodium valproate might cause seizures to come back sooner. There wasn't much information about side effects, and some side effects were similar for both medicines. Most of the studies were done well, but some had problems like not hiding which medicine people were getting. The results aren't very strong because of these issues. The studies mostly compared different treatments for diabetic eye disease or age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Bevacizumab, a medicine used to treat AMD, seemed to help people see better after 12 months. It helped them gain more lines on eye charts and reduced the chances of bleeding in their eyes. However, the evidence isn't very clear because the studies were small and some didn't report all the important information. Bevacizumab also seemed to help with another condition called proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR), reducing the risk of bleeding in the eye. output: This review looked at six studies involving 5152 people with multiple sclerosis (MS). The studies compared a medication called fingolimod with a placebo (a fake treatment) or other MS drugs. Most of the studies lasted for 24 months. Fingolimod helped reduce inflammation in the brain, making fewer people have relapses (when MS symptoms get worse) and fewer people have new MRI signs of inflammation. It also seemed to help with MRI scans showing less swelling in the brain. However, it didn't seem to prevent disability getting worse. Fingolimod worked better than a different MS drug called interferon beta-1a in the first year, but not in the second year. Fingolimod caused more side effects, especially at higher doses, which made some people stop taking it. Overall, fingolimod helps with inflammation but doesn't seem to make much difference in preventing disability. More studies are needed to fully understand its benefits and risks.

output:
This review looked at four studies involving 216 people who had cataracts and uveitis. The studies compared different types of artificial lenses (IOLs) used during cataract surgery. The studies had some problems, like not all participants finishing the full study and not always using the same way to measure success. 

In the biggest study, people got one of four types of IOLs: hydrophobic acrylic, silicone, HSM PMMA, or unmodified PMMA. After one year, about 90% of people saw at least one line clearer with any type of IOL. There wasn't much difference between hydrophobic acrylic and silicone IOLs. Hydrophobic acrylic IOLs were linked to fewer problems like posterior synechiae, but the link wasn't strong enough to be sure. 

The studies didn't find clear differences between other types of IOLs. Some studies looked at HSM PMMA and unmodified PMMA IOLs, but they weren't big enough to show clear results. Another study compared hydrophobic and hydrophilic acrylic IOLs, and found no clear difference in vision or other outcomes.

Overall, the studies don't give us a clear answer about which type of IOL works best for people with uveitis who have cataracts. More studies are needed to better understand the best options.

output:
This review looked at 21 studies involving 1,092,877 people in Africa, the Americas, and South-East Asia. These studies tested different kinds of unconditional cash transfers (UCTs), which give money to people without conditions. Most studies had some problems in how they were done, so we're not sure how good the results are. 

UCTs might make it less likely that people used health services in the past year, but the evidence isn't strong. Over the first two years, UCTs seem to help people feel healthier by reducing the chance of getting sick. They might also help people eat better by increasing their variety of foods. 

UCTs probably make it more likely that people are still going to school, especially for children. They might also help families spend more money on health care. However, we don't know if UCTs help with things like being undernourished, having enough money, or taking care of children. There's not enough clear evidence to say if UCTs work better than another kind of program called a conditional cash transfer (CCT).

Overall, UCTs seem to have some positive effects on health and education, but we need more research to be sure.

This review looked at seven studies involving 1924 elderly people and 740 others. Most studies tested different types of programs to help prevent elder abuse. Some studies were well-designed, but many were not. The evidence is not strong because the studies had some problems that made it hard to trust the results. 

Some studies found that programs helped reduce elder abuse, while others didn't. One study found that abuse might go down after a program, but another found more abuse in the program groups. Another study found that programs helped caregivers spot abuse better, but it's not clear if this meant more abuse or just better reporting. 

Overall, the evidence isn't strong enough to say for sure if these programs work. More high-quality studies are needed, especially from places with fewer resources. These studies should look at costs, how well the programs are implemented, and whether they help all kinds of people equally.

output: This review looked at six studies involving 681 adults and children with asthma flare-ups. The studies used different types of antibiotics, mostly macrolides, and compared them to a placebo. Most studies didn't report serious health problems like needing a hospital or intensive care unit. Some studies found that antibiotics helped reduce asthma symptoms and allowed people to breathe better. However, the studies had different ways of measuring success and some weren't done recently. The results aren't very strong because the studies had flaws and the effects weren't always clear. Overall, there's limited evidence that antibiotics might help asthma flare-ups, but the results aren't consistent across all studies. More research is needed to know if antibiotics really work and to make sure they don't cause problems.

output: This review looked at 13 studies with 2010 participants to see if helping people stop smoking before and after surgery works. Most studies were done well, but there weren't many, so we can't be sure about the results. Studies that gave people extra help like talking to a counselor or using medicine to quit smoking were more likely to help people stop smoking right before their surgery. This extra help also seemed to make it less likely that they would get sick after the surgery. But, studies that just gave people a little bit of help didn't seem to work as well. Some medicines like varenicline might help people stop smoking for a longer time, but they didn't seem to help much right before or after surgery. The best way to help people stop smoking seems to be giving them extra help starting about four to eight weeks before their surgery, having weekly counseling sessions, and using medicine to help. More research is needed to know the best way to do this.

output: This review looked at 10 studies comparing different ways to use fluoride to prevent white spots (dental lesions) on teeth during orthodontic treatment. The studies varied in how well they were done, so we can't be sure how reliable their results are. Some studies found that using a special fluoride foam every two months might help prevent these spots, especially after braces are put in. Other studies suggested that using a higher concentration of fluoride toothpaste might also work better than regular toothpaste. But other comparisons didn't show clear benefits. The studies also found that using fluoride varnish (a sticky substance put on teeth) wasn't clearly better than not using it. None of the studies looked at how much patients followed the fluoride instructions or if there were any side effects. Since the studies weren't always done the same way, we're not sure if the results would apply to everyone. More studies are needed to confirm these findings and to find the best way to prevent these spots during orthodontic treatment.

output: This review looked at 20 studies comparing different treatments for dental problems called periapical lesions. Most of the studies were not very good at making sure their results were fair. The studies didn't show that one type of surgery was better than another for healing these problems. However, they did find that people who had surgery often had more pain in the first week after the procedure. Some studies suggested that using a special material called MTA to fill the roots might help heal better than other materials. Using a tool called a laser to treat the problem didn't seem to help with pain. Other things like using a special kind of light during surgery or putting a special gel in the gums didn't seem to make much difference. Overall, the evidence isn't strong enough to give clear advice on which treatments work best. More research is needed to understand which methods are most effective and to make sure the results are reliable.

output:
This review looked at 20 studies with 2151 participants to see if certain treatments helped prevent something called 'transition to psychosis', which means moving from having milder mental health issues to more severe ones. The studies compared different treatments like amino acids, omega-3 fatty acids, and different types of therapy. 

For omega-3 fatty acids, the studies showed that people who took them were less likely to move to a more severe state compared to those who didn't take them. This was a bit better than taking a placebo, but the evidence isn't very strong because the studies weren't perfect.

Other treatments like adding amisulpiride or olanzapine to specific care packages, or using cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) with or without risperidone, didn't seem to help prevent the transition to psychosis. Some combinations of CBT and supportive therapy seemed to work a little better, but the evidence wasn't very strong.

Overall, the evidence suggests that omega-3 fatty acids might help prevent the transition to psychosis, but more research is needed to confirm this. Other treatments didn't show a clear benefit in preventing this transition.

For omega-3 fatty acids, the studies showed that people who took them were less likely to move to a more severe state compared to those who didn't take them. This was a bit better than taking a placebo, but the evidence isn't very strong because the studies weren't perfect.

Other treatments like adding amisulpiride or olanzapine to specific care packages, or using cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) with or without risperidone, didn't seem to help prevent the transition to psychosis. Some combinations of CBT and supportive therapy seemed to work a little better, but the evidence wasn't very strong.

Overall, the evidence suggests that omega-3 fatty acids might help prevent the transition to psychosis, but more research is needed to confirm this. Other treatments didn't show a clear benefit in preventing this transition.

output: This review looked at 35 trials that tested how well cocoa products help lower blood pressure. People took cocoa products with 30 to 1218 milligrams of flavanols (a type of antioxidant) every day for 2 to 18 weeks. The control group took something without flavanols or a lower amount of flavanols. The results showed that cocoa products helped lower blood pressure, especially in people who already have high blood pressure. The effect was small, about 2 mmHg lower in blood pressure. However, the effect wasn't seen in people with normal blood pressure. Some people had minor side effects like stomach problems or nausea, but it was rare. The review suggests that eating cocoa products might help lower blood pressure, but more research is needed to confirm these findings. It's important to note that the results might not apply to everyone, and longer studies are needed to see if cocoa helps prevent heart problems.

output: This review looked at 77 trials involving 40,249 women and their babies. Most of the trials were done in high-income and upper-middle-income countries. The main finding was that taking low-dose aspirin during pregnancy helped reduce some problems like pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, and small babies. It also helped prevent serious problems during pregnancy. However, it slightly increased the chance of heavy bleeding after birth and a rare condition called placental abruption. Overall, the benefits seem to outweigh the risks. More research is needed to find out if giving aspirin earlier in pregnancy helps even more. Also, it's not clear if higher doses of aspirin work better.

output:
This review looked at different ways to help prevent altitude sickness (AMS) before going to high altitudes. It included 20 studies with 1406 participants. Some methods like using a special machine to simulate altitude or a technique called remote ischaemic preconditioning didn't seem to help prevent AMS. But another method called positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) might help, though it's based on a small study. There's not much information about side effects from these methods.

For supplements and vitamins, taking certain things like antioxidants, medroxyprogesterone, iron, or Rhodiola crenulata didn't seem to help prevent AMS. However, taking erythropoietin might help, but the evidence isn't strong because the study had some problems. Ginkgo biloba didn't show clear results in preventing AMS, and there wasn't enough information about side effects.

When ginkgo biloba was taken with another medicine called acetazolamide, it seemed to help prevent AMS, but again, the evidence is not very strong. Taking medroxyprogesterone with acetazolamide didn't seem to help prevent AMS.

Overall, the evidence is mixed and not very strong. More studies are needed to better understand if these methods work and if they're safe. Clinicians should use caution and consider the quality of the evidence when recommending these methods.

output: This review looked at 54 studies that tested whether exercise helps people with knee osteoarthritis feel better. Most studies were well-designed, but some had problems like not hiding which treatment a person got. The studies showed that exercise helped reduce pain right away and also improved how well people could move their knees. It also seemed to help people's overall quality of life. About 1 in 4 studies didn't have big problems hiding which treatment people got. After the exercise ended, the benefits lasted for about 2 to 6 months. Some people might get a little bit of knee or back pain from the exercise, but nothing serious happened. The studies showed that people who did the exercise themselves usually got more pain relief and better movement than those who did it in a class or at home. While the effects weren't huge, they were still noticeable. Since most people knew which treatment they were getting, it's possible that they felt better just because they thought they were doing something helpful. Overall, the evidence suggests that exercise can help knee pain and movement in the short term, and these benefits last for a few months. More research is needed to confirm these findings.

output: This review looked at five studies that tested if training health professionals in cultural competence helps them better serve patients from diverse backgrounds, especially those from cultures different from their own. The studies involved about 3,300 health professionals and 8,400 patients. Most of the patients were from diverse cultural backgrounds, but the studies didn't always clearly define what that meant. The studies found that training in cultural competence didn't seem to help health professionals achieve specific goals like helping patients lower their cholesterol or lose weight. However, it did seem to help patients feel more comfortable and understood by their doctors. Some patients said they were happier with their doctor-patient interactions after the training. But the studies weren't perfect, and the results weren't strong enough to make a clear recommendation. More research is needed to see if these training programs work and to figure out the best way to do them.

This review looked at 12 studies involving 1554 people. Most studies looked at whether probiotics helped prevent diarrhea caused by radiation therapy or chemotherapy. For preventing radiation-induced diarrhea, there wasn't enough clear evidence to say if probiotics worked better than a placebo. Some studies suggested probiotics might help reduce the severity of diarrhea, but the evidence was not strong. For chemotherapy-induced diarrhea, the studies were too different to combine their results. Probiotics didn't seem to help much with chemotherapy-induced diarrhea either. 

Some studies found that probiotics might help reduce the need for medicine to treat diarrhea, but the evidence was not very strong. Overall, the studies showed that probiotics might help a little bit with preventing diarrhea, but the benefits weren't always clear. There wasn't enough evidence to say if probiotics cause any serious side effects. More research is needed to give us a clearer picture of whether probiotics are helpful for preventing or treating diarrhea caused by radiation or chemotherapy.

This review looked at five studies involving 368 people with pain in their kneecaps (PFPS). The studies were done in health clinics and with military recruits. Most of the studies had problems keeping things fair, like making sure neither the doctors nor the patients knew who got which treatment. Based on the limited information, we're not sure if knee braces, sleeves, or straps help with knee pain or make daily activities better. Here's what we know:

- Knee pain didn't seem to get much better with knee braces, sleeves, or straps compared to just doing exercises.
- People didn't have more trouble with sports or work after using knee braces, sleeves, or straps.
- Some people had minor problems like soreness or skin irritation from wearing knee braces or straps.
- Using knee braces or straps didn't seem to help more than just doing exercises.

Overall, the studies weren't very good at showing if knee braces or straps work for PFPS. We need better studies to find out if these devices help or not.

This review looked at 183 studies with 252,886 participants to see if macrolide antibiotics helped or hurt people. Most studies used these antibiotics to treat or prevent illnesses like colds, heart problems, breathing issues, stomach problems, and women's health issues. Many of the studies happened in hospitals where people get sick. Different kinds of macrolide antibiotics were studied, but azithromycin and erythromycin were used more often.

The studies found that people taking macrolide antibiotics were more likely to have some bad side effects, like feeling sick in their tummy, having diarrhea, and feeling queasy. These side effects were more common than with people who took a sugar pill instead. The chance of getting these side effects was about 1 in 10 for people taking macrolides compared to about 1 in 100 for those taking a placebo.

There wasn't much difference between different types of macrolide antibiotics or how they were taken. But people taking macrolides were more likely to have taste problems and hearing loss, though these weren't always clear. The antibiotics didn't seem to cause more heart or liver problems, but they didn't reduce coughing or the number of colds either. They also didn't make people more likely to die.

Some studies said there might be more resistant bacteria in people taking macrolides, but it wasn't always clear. Pharmaceutical companies often paid for the studies or gave money, which could affect the results. Many studies didn't report all the side effects clearly.

output: This review looked at five studies involving 71,458 women with uncomplicated pregnancies. Most studies had some issues with how they were done, so we can't be sure they were fair. Two studies compared how often women counted their baby's movements during pregnancy. One study found that women who counted their baby's movements more often didn't have more stillbirths or more cesarean sections. They did find that these women had less anxiety and their babies might be born a little lighter. Another study found that women who counted their baby's movements more often went to the hospital fewer times. But there wasn't enough information to know if this made a big difference. Some studies said that more babies at risk of problems were found in the group that counted movements more often, but this didn't lead to fewer babies dying or getting very sick. We don't have strong enough evidence to change how doctors do things based on these studies. More research is needed to see if counting your baby's movements helps.

output: This review looked at six studies that compared the safety and effectiveness of nurse practitioners (NPs) giving anesthesia to doctors doing it. Most studies found no difference in how safe or effective the two groups were. Some studies showed NPs might be safer, especially in places where doctors don't always check on them. But other studies found no clear difference. The studies had different ways of looking at the data, which made it hard to compare them. Some studies got money from companies that might have influenced their results. Because of these issues, we can't say for sure if NPs are better or worse at giving anesthesia. The studies were complicated and didn't always consider all the factors that could affect the results. So, we don't have enough clear evidence to say if NPs are better than doctors at giving anesthesia. More studies with better methods are needed to understand this better.

This review looked at 24 studies involving 10,056 women to see if antenatal (before birth) education about breastfeeding helped new mothers start and continue breastfeeding. Most studies came from countries like the USA, UK, Canada, and Australia. The studies didn't always measure the same things, so we couldn't combine all the data. 

For some types of education, there wasn't much difference in how long women breastfed or whether they started or continued breastfeeding. Some education programs seemed to help a little bit, but the results weren't clear. Other programs didn't seem to make a difference.

There was no strong evidence that any specific education program improved how long women breastfed or whether they started or continued. The studies had some flaws, like not making sure everyone knew who was getting the education. 

Overall, the evidence isn't strong enough to say that antenatal breastfeeding education helps. More research is needed, especially in lower income countries. More high-quality studies are needed to better understand the effects of these programs.

This review looked at 28 studies comparing different ways to keep patients asleep during surgery. Most of the studies used propofol and others used gases like sevoflurane, isoflurane, and desflurane. Many studies didn't clearly describe how they picked who got which treatment, which made it hard to know if the results are reliable. About half of the studies couldn't tell if the people giving out medicine knew who was getting which treatment, which might have affected the results. 

The studies mostly found that using propofol to keep patients asleep didn't make it more likely that they would have problems like confusion after surgery (postoperative delirium). But the evidence for this isn't very strong because the studies weren't very big or clear. There wasn't enough evidence to say if propofol kept people from having more problems after surgery (POCD) or if it changed how long they stayed in the hospital.

Some studies suggested that propofol might help with POCD, but the evidence wasn't very strong. There wasn't enough evidence to say if propofol or other medicines used to keep patients asleep changed how long it took for patients to wake up after surgery (length of stay in the PACU) or if it changed how long they stayed in the hospital.

Overall, the evidence isn't very strong about whether propofol or other medicines used to keep patients asleep affect these things. More studies are needed to get a clearer picture.

This review looked at 60 trials involving 3620 people with chronic rotator cuff problems. Most of the trials had low risk of bias, but some had unclear or high risk. Only one trial compared manual therapy and exercise to a placebo, and it showed that these treatments helped reduce pain and improve function more than the placebo. About 7 out of 10 people who got manual therapy and exercise said their condition improved, compared to about 4 out of 10 who got the placebo. The treatments caused some mild side effects like short-term pain after treatment.

However, other trials didn't find clear differences between manual therapy and exercise and other treatments like injections or surgery. Some trials suggested that combining manual therapy or exercise with other treatments might not offer extra benefits.

Overall, the evidence suggests that manual therapy and exercise can help with pain and function, but it's not clear if they're better than other treatments. More research is needed to confirm these findings and to see if different types of manual therapy or exercise work best. Future studies should compare these treatments to realistic placebos and have a strong reason for doing so.

output: This review looked at seven studies, mostly in children, to see if removing their tonsils and adenoids (a procedure called adeno-/tonsillectomy) helps reduce sore throats. In children, those who had the surgery had fewer sore throats overall, especially those who were more sick. They had about 0.6 fewer sore throats in the first year after the surgery compared to those who didn't have the surgery. However, the difference was small, and one sore throat often happened right after the surgery. For adults, the studies were shorter and mixed, so we can't be sure if the surgery helps. The surgery seems to help a bit in reducing sore throats, but the benefits are small. The surgery can cause some discomfort and a small risk of bleeding. More research is needed to know if the surgery is worth doing for sore throats.

output: This review looked at whether giving antibiotics later instead of right away helps with symptoms like fever, pain, and cough in people with certain types of respiratory infections. It included 11 studies with a total of 3555 participants. Most studies were done in doctor's offices or clinics. The studies found that giving antibiotics later didn't seem to make much difference in how sick people felt or how quickly they got better. However, it did help reduce the number of antibiotics given out. Patients who waited for antibiotics to start feeling better were just as satisfied as those who got them right away. The review suggests that waiting to give antibiotics might be a good idea for some people with respiratory infections because it can help stop the spread of bacteria that cause infections, which can lead to less antibiotic resistance. This means fewer people would get sick again from the same bacteria.
